verdict.root_cause: At 08:08:02Z platform-automation lowered the memory resource limit on the frauddetection-service workload to 200m. Roughly eighteen seconds later the service stopped doing useful work and entered a crash-restart loop: from ~08:08:20 to at least 08:16:19 the log contains nothing but repeated full JVM/OpenTelemetry-agent bootstrap sequences at ~60s intervals, with no application errors, exceptions, or stack traces to explain the termination, and no order-consumption records after the first restart. That signature — a JVM that starts, does no visible work, and dies silently without logging, immediately after its memory ceiling was tightened — is the classic pattern of a container being killed by the kernel for exceeding a ceiling that is now below the heap the JVM is configured to commit. The service is not failing on a bad code path; it is being denied the memory it needs and is killed for it, so the failing mechanism is memory exhaustion against the new limit. The span-derived call metrics being entirely absent (no error numerator and no total-calls denominator) is a downstream consequence: a process that never lives long enough to serve traffic emits no RPC spans.
verdict.reasoning: Three independent lines converge. (1) tr_4215e952dfd4 establishes that exactly one change landed in the window and it was a memory-limit reduction at 08:08:02Z; deploys, flag flips, and dependency bumps were each explicitly ruled out, so there is no competing local trigger. (2) tr_8d36cfc8aff2 dates the behavioural break to ~08:08:20 — eighteen seconds after the change — and characterises it as repeated JVM startup banners rather than degraded throughput inside one long-lived process, while ruling out application errors, dependency failures, business-logic faults, and a broken log pipeline. Crucially it found no exception or panic: the process is being killed from outside, not failing from within, which is what an external memory kill looks like from stdout. (3) tr_358bb2221bb0 and tr_f69cbcf7cffc both show the total-calls denominator is empty, not just the error numerator — the service is serving no traffic at all, which fits a process that never reaches readiness, and is inconsistent with a normal-traffic-with-errors state (explicitly ruled out in both). I classify this as resource_exhaustion rather than bad_config because the config edit is how it started while running out of memory against the ceiling is what is happening now; the request path is broken by the process dying, not by any value naming a wrong address, port or credential. Remediation is config_revert because restoring the prior limit (or raising it above the JVM's committed footprint) is what would actually stop the kills — a restart alone would only re-enter the loop, and a rollback has nothing to roll back to since no artifact changed.
open_questions: The OOM kill itself is inferred, not observed. kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total, last_terminated_reason, container_memory_working_set_bytes and the container memory limit series were never queried (tr_f69cbcf7cffc explicitly leaves the OOM hypothesis open). A single query for last_terminated_reason=OOMKilled would confirm or refute the mechanism outright.

The prior memory limit is not recorded (tr_4215e952dfd4), so the magnitude of the reduction is unknown and the correct value to revert to has to be determined from the JVM heap settings or from a healthy peer, not from the change record.

The recorded new value '200m' uses milli-unit notation, which is a CPU unit, not a memory unit. If the limit was written with a malformed or misinterpreted unit rather than merely lowered, the framing shifts toward a wrong value rather than a tight-but-intentional ceiling, and the fix differs (correct the unit vs. restore a number). This was not resolved.

The log result covers only 08:04–08:19 and the middle of the window was dropped (oldest 8 + newest 32 lines kept), so an error or exception in the dropped segment cannot be excluded, and it is unknown whether the restart loop continued past 08:16:19.

Why platform-automation made this change is unexamined — whether it was a policy rollout, an autoscaler/VPA recommendation, or a templating error determines whether reverting the limit will simply be re-applied by the same automation.

No evidence was gathered on whether other workloads received the same automated limit reduction; triage scoped this to one service, but the actor was automation, which typically acts on more than one target.
